title: Elastic safety-net autoscaler and tenant quarantine proposal
abstract: Sketch of a safety-net autoscaler for Dedicated capacity that preserves SLOs by combining a small global emergency pool, tenant-specific burst loans, and a soft quarantine mechanism that temporarily reins in noisy tenants without hard evictions.
background: We need an operationally simple autoscaling strategy that protects latency and tail-SLOs during demand surges while minimizing hard tenant evictions and revenue loss. Current Dedicated behavior leans toward either aggressive prewarm (expensive) or blunt eviction policies (customer-impacting). This doc proposes a middle path: an elastic safety net plus a tenant quarantine leash implemented as credit-based controls and opportunistic rebalancing.
problem_statement: During correlated spikes (e.g., product releases, promotions) our Dedicated pools face short-lived but high-intensity bursts. Without better controls we either: 1) overprovision to cover rare peaks, increasing unit cost; 2) throttle/evict tenants abruptly causing errors; or 3) accept degraded tail latency. We need an approach to smooth demand, favor latency SLOs for high-priority tenants, and provide predictable operational playbooks.
proposed_solution: Introduce an Elastic Safety Net Autoscaler (ESNA) composed of three coordinated pieces: a small global EmergencyPool (short-lived prewarmed capacity), a TenantBurstCredit system (per-tenant token buckets that allow controlled bursts and loans), and a SoftQuarantine flow (automated, reversible throttling with observability and notice). A lightweight Rebalancer agent will opportunistically migrate queued work between nodes to reduce hot spots. Control plane exposes policies per-tenant: priority band, max-burst, refill-rate, and quarantine thresholds. Default policy aims to keep P99 generation latency within SLO with minimal cost uplift.
architecture_notes: ESNA includes a global broker (control plane) that tracks credits and EmergencyPool state, a local agent on each Dedicated node that enforces token buckets and collects signals (queue depth, GPU utilization, KV-cache hit rate), and a Rebalancer that can shift low-priority work using warm cache hints. The control plane integrates with Redwood Console to surface per-tenant credit balance, quarantine history, and backoff recommendations.
how_it_behaves_in_examples: 1) Short spike: tenant A uses burst credits to exceed baseline throughput; credits drain and then refill over a decay window. No eviction. 2) Sustained surge beyond safe refill: when credits deplete and latency degrades, ESNA moves tenant to SoftQuarantine (progressive rate cap + reminder to customer). EmergencyPool may be used for a 2-5 minute runway while autoscaler boots additional capacity. 3) Multi-tenant incident: Rebalancer moves opportunistic batches from overloaded nodes to underutilized nodes; low-priority tenants see longer queue delays rather than hard errors.
user_stories: As a platform engineer I want a global EmergencyPool so short spikes don't trigger immediate evictions.
As an SRE I want per-tenant burst credits so noisy tenants can be temporarily isolated without losing traffic entirely.
As a product owner I want priority bands (Gold/Silver/Bronze) so customers with higher SLAs get preferential refill and emergency access.
As an operator I want automatic SoftQuarantine notifications surfaced in Console and to customers via webhooks so remediation is fast and visible.
requirements: R1: System must keep tail latency P99 within configured SLO for priority band Gold on 95% of incidents.
R2: EmergencyPool should be configurable per-region and capped at a percentage of total Dedicated capacity (default 5%).
R3: TenantBurstCredits must be viewable in Console and have audit logs for credit changes.
R4: SoftQuarantine must be reversible and must not perform hard VM/worker evictions without operator approval.
R5: Rebalancer must not relocate stateful caches unless warm cache hints exist; cold transfers must be deprioritized.
R6: All policy changes must be evaluable via rollout flags and observability dashboards before global enablement.
non_goals: NG1: This is not a wholesale replacement for long-term reserved capacity economics (Reserved/Committed contracts).
NG2: Not trying to solve model-level inefficiencies (prompt engineering, batching at the SDK level).
NG3: Not implementing preemptible burst VMs in first phase.
metrics: M1: P99 generation latency per priority band (baseline vs incident)
M2: % incidents where EmergencyPool prevented an eviction
M3: Average credit usage per tenant and credit refill rate
M4: Incidents with SoftQuarantine invoked and mean time to restore (MTTR)
M5: Cost delta vs baseline (delta in GPU-minutes due to EmergencyPool)
safety_and_fallbacks: - EmergencyPool acts as single-shot runway and has circuit-breaker thresholds to avoid sustained cost blowouts. - If EmergencyPool consumption exceeds X% in a rolling window, autoscaler falls back to conservative prewarm and operator alerts. - SoftQuarantine escalations include automatic rollback timers and operator manual override. - If Rebalancer introduces cache miss penalties > threshold, it backs off and marks nodes for 'no-relocate' for a cooldown period.
implementation_sketch: Phase 1: Credit ledger + local token-bucket enforcement + EmergencyPool orchestrator (start/stop small warm workers). Phase 2: Rebalancer with warm-hint protocol and Console integration + soft quarantine and customer notification flows. Phase 3: Policy tuning, per-tenant economics signals, and experiment to surface tradeoffs in Console and billing.
rollout_plan: 1) Internal dogfood in one region with non-critical tenants (2 weeks). 2) Expand to low-risk Dedicated pools and enable read-only Console views for customers (4 weeks). 3) Beta customers opt-in for SoftQuarantine testing (6 weeks). 4) Gradual global rollout with feature flag and monitoring gates (4-8 weeks). Rollback plan: feature flag off -> EmergencyPool drained -> credits disabled -> revert to existing autoscaler behavior.
ops_runbook: - Detection: Alert when credit drain rate > threshold or EmergencyPool usage > 30%. - First response: Notify owners, enable temporary rate caps for low-priority tenants, and spin EmergencyPool in region. - If quarantine triggered: send webhook to customer, enable backoff on SDK routes, and schedule 15 minute review. - Escalation: If MTTR > 30m or multiple regions impacted, open incident with SRE and Product on-call. - Post-incident: run postmortem, adjust refill rates, and consider permanent policy changes.
open_questions: Q1: What is the default size of EmergencyPool by region (2%, 5%, 10%)?
Q2: How should credits be purchased/charged — included in Dedicated commitment or as overage?
Q3: What customer-facing language and SLAs do we provide around SoftQuarantine (notice periods, retry semantics)?
Q4: Edge cases: how to handle tenants with very bursty embeddings workloads that bypass KV cache assumptions?
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: Customers perceive SoftQuarantine as silent throttling -> Mitigation: require notification webhook and Console banner before quarantine.
Risk: EmergencyPool increases unit cost -> Mitigation: make pool small, monitor cost delta, and gate by feature flag.
Risk: Rebalancer causes cache churn -> Mitigation: warm-hint protocol and conservative thresholds in Phase 1.
next_steps: Schedule architecture RFC with infra and serving-runtime teams, prototype credit ledger (in-memory ledger + periodic durability), and run chaos experiments on dogfood to validate P99 improvement. Prepare small UI mock for Console credit view and notification templates for customers.
